newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Budget bills update for Dec 11 - overview.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Budget bills update for Dec 11 - overview.

text.p: The Australian government needs more time to get its budget bills through, and on Wednesday afternoon it was negotiating with minority Senate parties to get that time.

The Senate has been spending so much time on the Telstra privatisation bill -- and it was still debating it at 0610 GMT (5.10 p.m.) -- that the remaining two days of sitting simply do not have enough time to finish the budget.
If they do not, then budget measures that were supposed to start on January 1 will be delayed maybe two months, costing perhaps hundreds of millions of Australian dollars.

"There's two full days' debate in the social security bills alone," said one Senate staffer, referring to the two bills that would cut social security entitlements. (See the accompanying report detailing all of the budget measures at risk.)
The problem has been that the minority parties have been so irritated by the likely passage of the Telstra bill that they have freely indulged in very lengthy debate on every proposed amendment.
According to one source, the government then put around a rumour that it might seek an extra week's sittings, which would have pleased no-one in the Senate.
The Labor party responded, according to the same source, by saying: "You'll get your budget bills."
On that basis, they are currently negotiating.
Apart from the continued passage of time, there have been no further developments on the budget bills, so the following summary of the fiscal situation largely repeats what we said on Tuesday.

The government promised a fiscal tightening in March, with the aim of cutting the underlying 1997/98 budget by A$8 billion. Treasurer Peter Costello announced measures in the August budget that would save A$7.2 billion in 1997/98. (This left A$800 million outstanding, and Prime Minister John Howard suggested earlier on Wednesday that there would be no further tightening.)

In the weeks after the budget it became clear that measures worth about A$2 billion in 1997/98 were doubtful, because both Labor and the Democrats would or might oppose them, leaving the government depending on the Greens or, more realistically, the Independents for passage.
Last week one of those contentious budget bills, containing measures worth about A$300 million in 1997/98, passed the parliament. It is the only major contentious budget bill to be dealt with so far.
The remainder -- worth roughly A$1.7 billion in 1997/98 -- are still waiting for Senate passage, with most of them scheduled to dealt with this week.
